# Sprint Biomechanics Introduction — checked transcript

- Course: Fundamentals of Sprinting | A Complete Biomechanics Course
- Lesson: 1 of 17, Jeff Moyer
- Video: https://player.vimeo.com/video/1115110104
- Course lesson: https://www.strengthcoachnetwork.com/learn/sprint-biomechanics-fundamentals/2A5V05F
- Video duration: 10:10
- Verification: Local faster-whisper small.en ASR was compared against the course transcript and the downloaded player captions; word-level agreement with the captions was 94.3%. Clear proper names were corrected; wording is lightly normalized. This is a reviewed machine transcript, not a certified verbatim record.
- Unresolved at 6:30–6:35: Both transcript sources misrecognize the precise elbow fracture term. The audio wording remains unclear and is marked below.

**[00:00]** Hey, thank you so much for purchasing the course. I wanted to put together this course for several reasons. One is I wanna try to preserve our history. I feel that we have more knowledge now than ever, but we don't know our past. We have more information than ever, but we don't have any knowledge and we lack a lot of sense. And because of this, I feel that there's a lot of confusion in our industry, right? We have a lot of monkey see, monkey do type of mentality of I see this coach doing it

**[00:32]** with these athletes on social media or at a seminar. And so I'm gonna just kind of plug and play, but not understand the context in which that exercise or method was developed and where it came from and how it was originally used with athletes and where it fit in the training program, right? We just kind of do things because it sounds sexy or it sounds all scientific-like. And the whole adage of if you don't know your history, you're doomed to repeat it, that's currently going on. I mean, a lot of the research now being done

**[01:04]** on biomechanics or sprinting is just proving things that was already studied and done back in the 60s, 70s and 80s. And that's one of the reasons why I wanted to build this course is because I want to show the science. I want to show the history of sports training that was done and a lot of it coming from the former Eastern Bloc countries and how detailed the science was and how it's still holding up to this day. And then not only that, I want to show practically how to apply those things, right?

**[01:35]** So we do a great job. We have a PhD in general fitness and training with athletes in the weight room, right? We know how to measure bar velocity, force plates, unilateral force plate measurements and all this stuff, RSI jumps and all this stuff is great. But then when it comes to now on the field movements and assessments, we have a very low level GED with that stuff. And the mechanism of injury a lot of times with athletes is not something here in the weight room.

**[02:06]** It's on the field. So let's get a better sense of how athletes move on the field, right? Our job is to improve our athletes movements on the field. So let's start there. Let's look at how they move and then let's kind of work backwards from there. And so I want to, with this course, be able to go through biomechanics and kinesiology of sprinting mechanics and then break it down as far as how to troubleshoot based off of, if we see a problem that's mechanically driven or if our athletes are lacking something,

**[02:36]** now what is the specific things that we can get into? And it's not so much a plug and play. I want to give more of a thought process to things, right? Because when looking at mechanics, it can get very overwhelming with the science and the Newtonian laws and physics and all that stuff. You get a lot of numbers, but then what do you do with it? How does that apply? What can I do as a coach to improve those specific things? And that's more or less what this course is going to be built on. I want to help coaches improve

**[03:07]** their problem solving ability and their toolbox that they have and not become reliant on AI softwares or computer programs. And I'm not saying that those are bad. I have those and I use those, but those are our means to justify what I'm already seeing. I use them to just quantify already what I'm seeing and when I break down and when I work with athletes and then I use it sometimes for selling mechanisms, selling to parents or showing to coaches and things using visualizations. But that's really it, that doesn't drive the bus.

**[03:38]** My eyes and my intuition in the toolbox that I've learned through 20 years of doing this is what drives the bus. And so this course, it's a part history lesson, but it's also then part practicality of like, okay, this is what biomechanics and technique analysis really looks like and this is now how we work to improve the issues that we see in front of us, both from an individual standpoint if we're working with just individual athletes or if we're working in a team setting, right?

**[04:08]** I want to have this be applicable to anyone and everyone on top of a return to play process because as I mentioned before, the mechanism of injury a lot of times is the mechanics of how the athlete moves and return to play processes usually forget the mechanics part and we just try to work on isolating whatever the joint is that the athlete hurt and then we do some kind of usually short to long return to play process and hey, well, let's look at how they move and let's work on the special strength exercise that can maybe help improve how they move

**[04:39]** and decrease the likelihood of injuries, right? If the number one predictor for a future injury is a previous injury, I think there's a lot of mechanisms for that but one of my big drivers is I think we don't look at how they move and I think that's one of the biggest reasons why the biggest predictor of an injury is a future injury. So let's look at how athletes move because ultimately that's our job. So I built this course for the coaches to, I want to teach you how to fish and then learn, you know,

**[05:11]** you guys can apply it to your own setting and hopefully help out. This journey of technique analysis really for me started back in about 2010 as I just took over, got done coaching college football and I took over working with a strength and conditioning for a high school football program and I took over right at the middle of August so football camp was just starting and the head football coach at the time was a former Division I Hall of Fame football player and also played in the NFL for about 10 years

**[05:43]** and was a predominant name in a lot of circles around the NFL and his son was the starting quarterback for the football team and going into the season had a little discomfort in his throwing arm but nothing crazy and by the third game of the season and I remember like yesterday, it was at night game and it was the third quarter, the quarterback, the boy went to go throw a pass and it looked like it got punted and all you heard was this loud scream and next thing you know, the boy's being pulled off the field,

**[06:16]** complaining about his elbow and at the time, I was working at a sports medicine orthopedic practice so my boss, the orthopedic surgeon, was on the field with me and immediately we got him into the practice and did an MRI and an X-ray and found that he had an [unclear elbow fracture term], he fractured the [unclear] plate in his right elbow and now I knew it was from his mechanics but I didn't have any background as far as how to assess one, the mechanics and two, how to practically improve it but what I did have at the time

**[06:46]** was Yosef Johnson or Ultimate Athlete Concepts who was a good friend of mine and he was mentored under Dr. Michael Yessis and being a football fan for, since I can remember, I knew the name Dr. Yessis because he worked with, back in the early 80s or late 80s, Todd Marinovich, also known as Robo-Quarterback and I remember seeing specials and videos on Doc working with him and the story went with Todd

**[07:17]** of how special the training was and how he was this just freak athlete and so I asked Joseph that would Doc be interested in possibly working with this boy and Doc said yes and so once the boy had surgery and the pin was taken out of his elbow, we then flew out to San Diego where Doc lives and we got to work. Right before we went, we sent Doc some game footage and some practice footage

**[07:47]** of the quarterback throwing so that way he had an understanding of the boy's throwing mechanics and as soon as we sat on Doc's couch he went, you have this, this, this, are wrong, your sequences is wrong and here's how we're going to improve it and about 20 minutes later we went to a field and we started getting to work on running, cutting and throwing mechanics and then special exercises to help improve the learning process of the new mechanical changes but also to improve the physical abilities as to relate that

**[08:18]** and I was blown away with Doc's knowledge of biomechanics but also now his knowledge of motor learning and how to correct someone's errors in their movement and that was when, again, a light bulb moment or light bulbs moment for me because that now really changed that, okay, we should be assessing how athletes move and then maybe kind of start backwards from there or it should be definitely part of the process and so I became the return to play specialist

**[08:50]** at the sports medicine orthopedic practice that I worked at and that was part of my job. If an athlete came in with throwing shoulder issues from throwing once the inflammation and the pain went down and he started going back to a return to play throwing program, I started assessing their throwing mechanics and same with runners and every other kind of athletes and from a performance standpoint it got them bigger, faster, stronger in their mechanics but then from a injury prevention standpoint

**[09:20]** it now decreased the likelihood of them coming back which, again, the biggest predictor for future injuries and so that has been my journey for the last 15 years now and I want to, this course is a labor of love of mine from that moment I sat on Dr. Yessis' couch and then also a love letter to Doc because Dr. Yessis unfortunately passed away a couple of years ago

**[09:51]** and his knowledge and expertise I don't think is fully appreciated and I want to share the things that I have learned and both practically and theoretically from Doc and how it applies and I want to spread the word of Dr. Yessis so here we are.

13	
14	# Degeneracy Precedes Dexterity; Abundance Precedes Adaptability
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors' compact statement of why a wide solution set matters (Myszka et al., 2023a). Two supporting terms:
17	
18	- **Degeneracy** — "the ability of elements that are structurally different to perform the same function or yield the same output" (Edelman & Gally, 2001). Different configurations, same outcome.
19	- **Abundance** — having access to more potential ways of coordinating movement-system components to solve problems. More *usable* degrees of freedom.
20	
21	The claim is directional: you cannot be adaptable to a problem you have only one answer for, so abundance is the precondition. Increased variability in coordination and control strategies is fundamentally linked to skill adaptation (Orth et al., 2017), because it supports the search and exploration through which a fitting solution is found.
22	
23	**Why it works** — Since no two problems are ever the same, a single grooved solution is a bet that the next problem resembles the last. Having more usable degrees of freedom means the player can transition into a different pattern when it does not (Gray, 2021). Fixation on one prescribed way of behaving is therefore not safety, it is fragility.
24	
25	**When to apply** — Justifying why practice should widen rather than narrow a player's repertoire, and why a coach should tolerate — actively pursue — movement variability, novelty and unorthodoxy rather than coaching them out. It is the theoretical partner to [[claim--prescriptive-coaching-narrows-adaptability]], which supplies the evidence, and it explains the mechanism behind [[principle--variability-overuse-hypothesis]].
26	
27	**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: degeneracy is well-established in biology and the reasoning is sound, but "abundance precedes adaptability" is the authors' own formulation and the ordering has not been demonstrated experimentally in football. More options is also not unconditionally better — abundance must be *usable* and *functional*, and a player with many solutions and no attunement to which one fits is not dexterous, only erratic. There is a real question, unresolved here, about whether a beginner needs some stability before abundance helps.
28	
29	**Example** — The book's illustration is two unrelated Sanders. Barry, described as having "moves on moves," solving apparently unsolvable problems by whatever strategy the moment allowed. Deion, playing shutdown corner, elite punt returner, and roughly half his team's offensive snaps in 1996 — and an NFL and MLB game on the same day. The point is not the highlight reel; it is that both were valuable *because* their toolbox was wide.
30

13	
14	# How to Watch Film
15	
16	**What it is** — The practical method for ecologically-informed performance analysis.
17	
18	**Live analysis is not enough.** The complexity of the problems, and of the solutions organised against them, makes real-time assessment next to impossible if you want an accurate reading. Analysis happens on video.
19	
20	**Watch widely.** Myszka's practice with a new NFL player is to watch **every single snap the player has taken in the league** (via NFL+ or NFL Rewind), then, depending on age and status, college film — even highlights — and sometimes high school. The rationale: you cannot determine where a player should go without unpacking how their movement skill came to be. Trends across a career are visible through the context-content lens that are invisible in a season.
21	
22	**Watch each play from as many vantage points as possible** — sideline, endzone, all-22 — and **at various speeds** — full, half, super slow motion. Cross-checking across conditions is what keeps a detail from being an artefact of one angle.
23	
24	**Two honesty rules the chapter insists on:**
25	
26	1. **Nonlinearity is real.** A player highly attuned one day can be overwhelmed by similar problems the next, for any number of reasons. Minor changes in the problem can produce dramatic changes in the solution, and vice versa.
27	2. **Absence of evidence is not evidence.** No two problems are the same and some problems the player has simply never faced. **Do not fret if you finish an analysis without enough to make a proclamation, good or bad.** Saying "I have not seen this player solve that problem" is a legitimate finding — and it is often the most actionable one, because it names an exposure gap ([[case-study--tight-end-punt-coverage-exposure-gap]]).
28	
29	**Why it works** — Breadth substitutes for the experiment you cannot run. You cannot present a player with a controlled problem set, so you find the range of problems they have already met.
30	
31	**When to apply** — Any serious individual analysis. The volume prescription is the part most people skip and the part that produces the trend.
32	
33	**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is one practitioner's method, offered without validation, and the authors concede it "can all sound quite daunting and may seem like overkill." Watching every career snap is not feasible for most staff at most levels, and there is no guidance here on what a reduced version preserves. Access also constrains it — what film you can get depends on your role. Treat the *principles* (multiple angles, multiple speeds, breadth over depth, comfort with an inconclusive verdict) as the transferable part.
34	
35	**Example** — A staff with two hours per player should spend them on twelve plays from three angles rather than one play frame by frame. The trend is the finding; the frame is the illustration.
36

# How to Watch Film

**What it is** — The practical method for ecologically-informed performance analysis.

**Live analysis is not enough.** The complexity of the problems, and of the solutions organised against them, makes real-time assessment next to impossible if you want an accurate reading. Analysis happens on video.

**Watch widely.** Myszka's practice with a new NFL player is to watch **every single snap the player has taken in the league** (via NFL+ or NFL Rewind), then, depending on age and status, college film — even highlights — and sometimes high school. The rationale: you cannot determine where a player should go without unpacking how their movement skill came to be. Trends across a career are visible through the context-content lens that are invisible in a season.

**Watch each play from as many vantage points as possible** — sideline, endzone, all-22 — and **at various speeds** — full, half, super slow motion. Cross-checking across conditions is what keeps a detail from being an artefact of one angle.

**Two honesty rules the chapter insists on:**

1. **Nonlinearity is real.** A player highly attuned one day can be overwhelmed by similar problems the next, for any number of reasons. Minor changes in the problem can produce dramatic changes in the solution, and vice versa.
2. **Absence of evidence is not evidence.** No two problems are the same and some problems the player has simply never faced. **Do not fret if you finish an analysis without enough to make a proclamation, good or bad.** Saying "I have not seen this player solve that problem" is a legitimate finding — and it is often the most actionable one, because it names an exposure gap ([[case-study--tight-end-punt-coverage-exposure-gap]]).

**Why it works** — Breadth substitutes for the experiment you cannot run. You cannot present a player with a controlled problem set, so you find the range of problems they have already met.

**When to apply** — Any serious individual analysis. The volume prescription is the part most people skip and the part that produces the trend.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is one practitioner's method, offered without validation, and the authors concede it "can all sound quite daunting and may seem like overkill." Watching every career snap is not feasible for most staff at most levels, and there is no guidance here on what a reduced version preserves. Access also constrains it — what film you can get depends on your role. Treat the *principles* (multiple angles, multiple speeds, breadth over depth, comfort with an inconclusive verdict) as the transferable part.

**Example** — A staff with two hours per player should spend them on twelve plays from three angles rather than one play frame by frame. The trend is the finding; the frame is the illustration.

# Sprint Problem-Solving Loop: Watch the Movement, Then Work Backwards

**What it is** — Moyer's organising idea for the whole course. Start with **how the athlete actually moves on the field**, not with the weight room or a drill menu, and work backwards: **observe the sport movement → name the constraint → intervene → look again**. The constraint can be **technical** (a sequencing error) or **physical** — his Live 2 example is a poor frontside/knee-drive action that may be a weak hip-flexor/lower-abdominal contribution rather than a coaching problem, so the fix is strength work for that joint action, not another cue. His one-line version from Live 1: *"drills are meant for solving problems — if you don't do an assessment, what problem are you trying to solve?"* Technology (video software, force plates) is there to **quantify what the eye already saw** and to sell the plan to coaches and parents; it does not "drive the bus."

**Why it works** — It forces the intervention to answer a named fault, so every drill has a reason and a test. The mechanism is ordinary diagnostic logic, not a sprint-specific finding. Moyer's own framing — that the weight room is where staffs hold a "PhD" and on-field movement is where they hold a "GED" — is a provocation, not a measured claim. Note the **recheck step is thin in the transcript**: it appears mainly as his demand, in Live 2, to "show me the before, tell me the intervention, show me the after," rather than as a defined retest protocol.

**When to apply** — Any speed block where drills were chosen before anyone filmed the athletes. A skill player whose 10-yard time stalls while his lifts climb. An RTP athlete cleared on tissue criteria who has not been filmed sprinting. Deciding whether a mechanics fault gets a cue or a strength exercise.

**When NOT to apply** — The loop presumes the observer can reliably see the constraint; Moyer's eye rests on 20 years and a mentorship with Michael Yessis, and he offers no reliability data for it. For a new staff member, "trust your eye over the software" is the wrong starting rule — use the video to *train* the eye. And for a large team with limited coaching time, a sound general speed program run for everyone may beat individual diagnosis for most athletes; the loop earns its cost on the athletes whose times or injury history say something is wrong.

**Example** — A slot receiver with a slow first 10 yards. Filming shows a low, short knee drive. Rather than adding A-skips, the staff checks whether hip-flexor strength and endurance at the relevant range are the limit, adds that work for four weeks, and refilms the same start from the same camera spot.

**Related** — [[heuristic--sprint-video-setup-stationary-camera]] — how to shoot the "observe" and "recheck" footage so they are comparable. [[claim--hip-flexor-fatigue-degrades-sprint-mechanics]] — the physical-limit example he leans on.

# Return to Play Should Examine the Movement Pattern Present at Injury

**What it is** — Moyer's claim: **the mechanism of injury is often the way the athlete moves**, yet return-to-play processes usually isolate the injured joint, restore tissue capacity, and progress a short-to-long running program without ever filming how the athlete runs, throws or cuts. His Live 1 line: *"you can have a great 10-by-10 running program, but if they run like shit you're just going to have another chance of getting hurt again."* He goes further: he suspects the reason **previous injury is the strongest predictor of future injury** is that the faulty movement is never addressed.

**Why it works** — The logic: if a movement fault loaded the tissue to failure once, a stronger tissue running the same pattern is still exposed. That is plausible, but **every causal link here is asserted, not shown**. The "previous injury predicts injury *because* we ignore movement" step is Moyer's inference; previous injury predicts re-injury through many routes (incomplete healing, scar tissue, deconditioning, early return, structural change). His evidence is clinical experience as an orthopaedic-practice RTP specialist and one case — a 16-year-old quarterback's elbow fracture on a throw, followed by surgery, rehab and eight months of mechanics work with Yessis — where all three changed at once.

**When to apply** — Late-stage RTP for a hamstring strain in a skill player: film the athlete sprinting before clearance and compare with pre-injury footage if it exists. A second soft-tissue injury in the same region. A throwing-arm injury with no contact mechanism. Add a filmed movement check to the RTP criteria, alongside, not instead of, tissue and capacity criteria.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a reason to delay tissue-based progression or to override the medical team. Many good RTP frameworks already include movement-quality checks, so the specific add here is **filming the movement that injured the athlete**, not "look at movement" in general. Contact injuries (a tackle to the knee) have no running-mechanics cause to correct. And changing mechanics late in rehab adds a new motor-learning load at the moment the athlete is least robust; timing matters.

**Example** — A corner strains his hamstring at top speed. Tissue criteria are met at week four. Before clearance, the staff films a 30-yard fly from the side and sees him landing well in front of the hips with a long swing-leg lever. They keep the RTP running progression but add targeted technical work and refilm before full practice.

**Related** — [[heuristic--sprint-problem-solving-loop]] — the general loop this applies to rehab. [[heuristic--sprint-video-setup-stationary-camera]] — how to capture comparable footage.

# Judge a Sprint Method by the Population It Was Built On

**What it is** — The one coaching principle worth keeping from Moyer's two hours of Soviet history. The Soviet system **classified athletes by performance standards** (third class up to Master of Sport, with fixed marks such as a 10.3 s 100 m for Master of Sport, as Moyer reads them from a 1981–84 table) and ran both **training and research within a class**. So a Soviet paper would state that its subjects were Class I or Master of Sport athletes. Moyer contrasts this with much Western work "done on 19 recreational athletes, or five soccer players." Two practical halves: **check who a method or study was built on**, and **group your own athletes by physical preparedness**, not by position or talent alone.

**Why it works** — Training responses differ with preparedness: what moves a novice may do nothing for a trained sprinter, and the reverse. Classification gives like-for-like groups, so the training dose and the research result both mean something for the next athlete in that class. The principle is sound. The history behind it is Moyer's narration and is **not verified here**; the Soviet results also rested on state compulsion, a huge talent funnel and pharmacology, which he acknowledges only in part.

**When to apply** — Reading a sprint-training study before adopting its method: were the subjects trained, and faster or slower than your roster? Building speed groups in the summer: group by measured sprint and strength qualities, not position. Moyer's Live 1 aside fits football well: many team-sport athletes are highly skilled but **physically underprepared** relative to their skill (his basketball example), and classifying by physical preparation exposes that gap.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not import Soviet classification standards themselves; they were built for track athletes in a different system and era. Do not discard research on recreational subjects outright; for many physiological questions it is the only evidence and may still transfer. And classification by one test (a 40 time) can misgroup athletes whose limits are different; use more than one quality.

**Example** — A study shows resisted-sled work improved 10 m times in untrained university students. Before giving the protocol to a group of 4.4-second defensive backs, the staff asks whether any trained-sprinter data exist, and pilots it on one speed group while keeping a comparison group.

**Related** — [[principle--know-a-sprint-drills-origin-before-copying-it]] — the same appraisal applied to drills. [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]] — Bompa's case for grouping by training age rather than chronological age; agreement.

# Essential vs. Non-Essential Variables in Sprint Observation

**What it is** — Moyer's bridge from Bernstein to what a coach should watch and coach in a sprint. Bernstein: to solve a motor problem the organism separates **essential variables** (actively controlled, protected against environmental disturbance) from **non-essential variables** (allowed to yield and adapt) — "active toward the former, reactive toward the latter." Verkhoshansky, Bernstein's student, renamed these **key movements** (which produce the power output of the skill) and **secondary movements** (which assist them). Moyer's application:

- **Coach the key movements; let the secondary ones vary.** In sprinting he names three key movements (knee drive, pawback, ankle extension) and treats the arms as secondary.
- **"We have to coach to something."** Against a purely self-organising, constraints-only approach, he argues there is no ideal model but there *are* key actions every good sprinter shares.
- **His reading of Bernstein's blacksmith:** the hammer took 100 different paths, but the **same joint actions** (shoulder, elbow, wrist) occurred each time. Trajectory varies; joint actions do not.

**Why it works** — It gives the observer a filter: variation in a secondary movement is noise to be tolerated, variation in a key movement is a fault to address. That matches Bernstein's idea and is consistent with the variability literature. **The list of what counts as "key" in sprinting is Moyer's judgement**, inherited from Verkhoshansky and Yessis, not an empirically derived set. His blacksmith reading is an interpretation; the ecological camp would say joint-action invariance at that coarse level is compatible with their view, so the disagreement is narrower than he presents.

**When to apply** — Deciding what to cue after watching a player sprint. Settling staff arguments about "ugly" sprinters: if the key actions are sound, leave the style alone. Explaining to a skill coach why a player's odd arm carriage is not the priority.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a licence to groove one technique: he concedes there is no ideal model and everyone runs differently. It is sprint-specific; in football, reactive tasks (pursuit angles, cuts) have different essentials, often perceptual, that this framework does not cover. And he cites Rob Gray as "late to the game" on coaching to something; that is his characterisation of a debate, not a settled result.

**Example** — Two receivers both have wild arm action. One also lands with a straight, stiff-kneed reach and slow ground contacts; the other has a fast, high knee drive and a quick down-and-back strike. The framework says fix the first receiver's leg action and leave the second one's arms alone.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]] — the key movements and the global views they build. [[principle--functional-variability]], [[principle--degeneracy-precedes-dexterity]] — agreement that variability is functional. [[claim--prescriptive-coaching-narrows-adaptability]], [[principle--soft-assembly-and-learner-centred-coaching]] — tension: Myszka would warn that coaching "key movements" narrows solutions. [[principle--repetition-without-repetition]] — Moyer says he dislikes the phrase while using its idea.

# Arm Action Is a Secondary Movement in Sprinting — Don't Over-Coach It

**What it is** — Moyer's position: the arms are a **secondary movement**. Their main job is to counter the rotation of the hips; they can **inhibit** force production if badly disordered, but they do not produce the forward force. When a parent says "my kid runs weird, look at his arms," he looks first at the **ankles and hips**, which usually explain the arms, and then at the athlete's sport (tennis and lacrosse players, used to holding an implement, often run with odd arms). His line: *"if arms were so important, drummers would be the fastest runners in the world."* He coaches arms rarely, and mostly for football players he does not want thinking about their arms.

**Why it works** — Follows from the essential/secondary split: fix the source (leg and pelvis action) and the arms reorganise. That is plausible, but **Moyer offers no study**; he says he has not seen one showing arm work improves times.

**The dispute (recorded in Live 2)** — A participant's track coach, whom he describes as brilliant, does the opposite: he cues arms first ("pull your arms through faster") because athletes can adjust arms consciously and the legs follow. The participant says both approaches get results. Moyer concedes "results matter" and does not claim the coach is wrong; his counter is that arm cues are **internal cues** and he questions their retention a week later, preferring external constraints such as wickets. So the live disagreement is about **what to cue**, not about whether arms produce force.

**When to apply** — Triage after filming: when both arms and legs look poor, start with the legs. Screening athletes from implement sports. Keeping football players' attention off their arms in position-specific speed work.

**When NOT to apply** — When the arms are grossly disordered (crossing midline, locked), they may be the constraint and worth direct work, which Moyer allows. When an athlete demonstrably responds to an arm cue and holds it across sessions, the result beats the theory. And for acceleration-heavy starts in football, arm drive's role in the first steps is not addressed in this lesson.

**Example** — A freshman running back swings his arms across his body. Film shows he lands in front of his hips with a slow, low knee drive. The staff works on his leg action first; three weeks later, refilming shows the arm swing has narrowed without any arm cue. If it had not, arm work would be the next step.

**Related** — [[framework--essential-vs-nonessential-variables-in-sprint-observation]] — the framework this claim comes from.

# Sprint Muscles Work Like Dimmers, Not Switches

**What it is** — Yessis's teaching point, passed on by Moyer: during the sprint cycle muscles do not snap on and off. They **dim up** as a joint action approaches, peak, and **dim down** as the limb passes the point where the opposing group must take over. The hamstrings, for example, build tension in mid-to-late swing to stop the thigh and pull the leg down and back, stay active through early stance, then fade once the thigh is behind the pelvis so the hip flexors can load and drive it forward. Moyer shows a Soviet EMG timing chart beside a 2017 review of sprint EMG studies and says the two patterns look very similar.

**Why it works** — Graded, overlapping activation is well supported by the sprint EMG literature. Moyer's mechanism — "we can't have muscles on opposite sides of a joint both maximally contracted; something has to calm down" — is **asserted, not shown**, and is too absolute: co-contraction around the knee and ankle in stance is real and useful for joint stiffness. # EMG Timing Shortlists Exercises; It Does Not Prove Transfer

**What it is** — Moyer uses sprint EMG timing charts (a Soviet chart and a 2017 review) to decide which muscles work in which phase, and so which exercises to pick. In Live 2 he states the limit himself: the chart **"shows muscle activation, but it doesn't tell you what type of muscular contraction it is."** The heuristic: use EMG timing to **shortlist** exercises whose joint action, range and timing match the sprint phase; then judge them on whether they change the sprint.

**Why it works** — EMG timing tells you *when* a muscle is electrically active. Transfer depends on much more: contraction type (the whole hamstring debate is about this), velocity, range, load, and the coordination of the whole movement. An exercise that lights up the same muscle in the same window can still train a different quality. This is standard caution in the EMG literature, not a Moyer-specific finding.

**When to apply** — A vendor or social-media post claims an exercise "activates the hamstrings like sprinting." Building a hamstring RTP progression and deciding which exercises earn a place. Reading any EMG study used to justify a drill.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a reason to ignore EMG: for identifying which muscles are working in a phase, it is the best cheap evidence there is. Moyer also leans on transfer arguments from Bondarchuk and Verkhoshansky (dynamic correspondence) elsewhere in the course; this entry is about the EMG step only. Whether a given exercise transfers is ultimately an outcome question on your athletes.

**Example** — Nordic curls show high hamstring EMG. A staff uses that to keep them in a hamstring program, but does not claim they train the late-swing sprint action; for that they add a sprint-specific exercise and track top-speed mechanics and times on film.

# Sprint Joint Actions and Muscles, Phase by Phase

**What it is** — Moyer's (and Yessis's) upright-sprint map of what the pelvis, hip, knee and ankle do in each phase, and which muscles are dimming up or down. Summarised from Lesson 4, cross-checked against its rework in Live 2:

| Phase | Pelvis | Hip | Knee | Ankle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Toe-off** | Anterior tilt (erectors) | Extension; glutes/hamstrings **dimming down**, hip flexors building tension to stop the thigh going further back | Slight flexion; quads roughly isometric | Plantar flexion (gastrocnemius, soleus) |
| **Early swing** | Posterior tilt begins (abdominals) | Flexion (iliopsoas, rectus femoris) | Flexion, largely passive, so the leg folds into a **short lever** | — |
| **Mid swing** | Posterior tilt (abdominals assist) | Flexion carried mainly by **momentum** of the initial contraction; hamstrings start building tension to stop the thigh | Extension as the shin swings out | — |
| **Late swing** | Anterior tilt (erectors) | Extension, down and back; **glute max and hamstrings most active** | Shin reaching toward contact | Plantar flexion |
| **Stance** | Anterior tilt | Extension; glutes/hamstrings working eccentric to quasi-isometric | Flexion; quads quasi-isometric to resist collapse | Plantar flexion; tibialis, gastrocnemius, soleus act as brakes |

Two add-ons from Live 2. **"There is no neutral pelvis"** — the pelvis should tilt anterior and posterior each stride; the question is the degree and whether the athlete controls it (his contrast: a hypermobile 14-year-old with large uncontrolled tilt). And in **acceleration** the hip does not extend as far behind the body, and glutes, hamstrings and calves contribute more to push-off.

**Why it works** — Knowing the joint action, its range and which muscles are loading lets you pick exercises that match a phase and diagnose whether a fault is technical or a strength deficit. The structure is standard gait-cycle kinesiology; the muscle roles are broadly consistent with sprint EMG data. Details below are where Moyer's version is loose.

**When to apply** — Building special-strength exercises for a phase (hip-flexor work through the toe-off-to-mid-swing range; hamstring work in the late-swing range). Explaining to a skill coach why a player's knee drive is low. Checking an RTP exercise list covers the ranges the injured tissue works through in sprinting.

**When NOT to apply** — **Do not quote this table as anatomy of record.** The lesson contains errors that are Moyer's, not the transcript's (they recur in Live 2): at stance he credits **glutes and hamstrings** with *anterior* pelvic tilt, although his own opening definition lists them as *posterior* tilters; he places plantar/dorsiflexion at the subtalar joint (it is the talocrural joint); and his late-swing knee is described as "flexion, quads isometric," which reads like stance, not swing. The lesson header also notes anatomical terms were standardised from context. It is an **upright-sprint** map; acceleration and football-specific starts differ. And it is qualitative: no joint angles or velocities are given beyond the contested knee figure.

**Example** — A tight end has a low, slow knee drive. The map says the thigh is driven from behind the body by the hip flexors, then carried by momentum with abdominal help. The staff adds hip-flexor work that starts from a hip-extended position and lower-abdominal posterior-tilt work (Moyer cites Yessis's reverse crunches), then refilms.

**Related** — [[principle--sprint-muscles-work-as-dimmers-not-switches]] — the activation pattern behind the table. [[claim--no-knee-extension-at-sprint-toe-off]] and [[claim--hamstrings-not-purely-isometric-in-late-swing]] — the two contested cells. [[claim--hip-flexor-fatigue-degrades-sprint-mechanics]], [[claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]] — claims built on this map.

# Hamstrings Are Not Purely Isometric in Late Swing (Contested)

**What it is** — Moyer's position in a live debate. One camp (he names Frans Bosch and "research out of Holland," using animal and computer-modelling work) holds that the hamstrings act **quasi-isometrically** through swing, with the tendon doing the lengthening and shortening. Moyer says there is "enough evidence" that they are **not fully isometric**: he accepts a quasi-isometric component but argues for real **eccentric and concentric** phases — eccentric to stop the thigh in mid-to-late swing, then pulling the leg down and back (pawback). He cites a 2020 review, **unnamed in the transcript**, and in Live 2 a study stating the hamstrings "do not behave isometrically during the swing phase." His practical conclusion: train the hamstrings through their sprint range with the eccentric-to-concentric switch that he links to hamstring strains.

**Why it works** — If the muscle fascicles do change length meaningfully, isometric-only training would miss the eccentric braking and the fast switch to shortening in the injury-prone window. **His main argument does not settle this.** "Two joints are moving, so the muscle can't be isometric" is about the **muscle-tendon unit**, whose lengthening nobody disputes; the Bosch/van Hooren position is about the **fascicles**, with the tendon absorbing the length change. So he argues past the other camp. The question turns on fascicle-level data during high-speed sprinting, which are scarce.

**When to apply** — Designing hamstring prevention or RTP loading for football speed positions: include both eccentric-biased work in long lengths and fast, sprint-range hip-extension work, rather than betting on one contraction type. Evaluating a coach or product that says "hamstrings are isometric, so only train isometrics."

**When NOT to apply** — Do not present either side as settled to the medical team. Moyer's own sources are unnamed, so his "enough evidence" cannot be checked from this course. The practical overlap is large: both camps load the hamstrings at long lengths and high speed, so the debate changes emphasis more than program content. Link to injury mechanism (the eccentric-to-concentric switch) is plausible and widely held but still **not a proven cause**.

**Example** — An RTP safety's late-stage program keeps heavy isometric holds at long lengths *and* adds fast single-leg hip-extension and supervised top-speed running, rather than choosing one side of the argument.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-joint-actions-by-phase]] — the late-swing cell this concerns. [[heuristic--emg-timing-shortlists-exercises-it-does-not-prove-transfer]] — why EMG timing charts cannot resolve contraction type.

# No Full Knee Extension at Sprint Toe-Off (Contested)

**What it is** — Moyer's firm position in Live 2: **"there is no knee extension when we sprint — the knee should not extend."** At toe-off the knee stays slightly flexed and the push comes through the **hip and ankle**; the knee is roughly "frozen" from touchdown to toe-off. Details from the exchange:

- He cites a *Soviet Sports Review* article: extending the knee from **164° to 168°** "to its full capacity is a useless movement," so the knee angle at the end of takeoff at maximum speed **should not exceed 165°**. He then refuses to give ranges to coaches, so they do not chase a number.
- **Acceleration:** the first step may extend; **from step two on** it should not fully extend either.
- **Diagnosis:** visible knee extension means the athlete is not using the ankle well — "weak in the calves and feet" — and it costs energy and creates "leaping."
- He names the rival idea directly: **"delayed knee extension,"** attributed to David Grey and Joel Smith, which he says "doesn't make sense."

**Why it works** — The argument is energetic: once the leg is nearly straight, further knee extension adds little push-off length and wastes time on the ground, while hip and ankle extension do the propulsive work. That is reasonable for **upright** sprinting. The **causal diagnosis** ("extension means weak calves") is **untested** — it is Moyer's clinical inference, and other causes (posture, intent, fatigue, coaching cues) are not considered.

**Why contested** — Moyer names an opposing school. The Live 2 "pushback" was mostly participants **checking their understanding** ("even as early as step two?") and paraphrasing back in agreement, not recorded disagreement. The contest lies in the wider field: early acceleration steps commonly show near-full knee extension at toe-off in fast athletes, and "delayed knee extension" is a live coaching model. His step-two rule is stricter than much acceleration practice.

**When to apply** — Upright, flying sprints: a clearly locked knee at toe-off, with long ground contacts and a bounding look, is worth investigating, starting with calf and foot strength. Watching a player who "leaps" rather than runs at top speed.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not coach football players out of knee extension in the first steps of a start, where force needs pushing horizontally over longer contacts; the course gives no acceleration data to back the step-two rule. Do not apply the 165° figure as a threshold; it rests on one translated article no one can easily check, and Moyer himself warns against it. And do not assume the calf is the cause without testing it.

**Example** — A linebacker's 20-yard fly shows a straight knee at toe-off and a floaty stride. Before cueing, the staff tests single-leg calf strength and finds a large deficit on one side from an old ankle sprain; that becomes the first target. His 10-yard start, which also shows extension on steps one to three, is left alone.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-joint-actions-by-phase]] — the toe-off cell this disputes. [[claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]] — the ankle claim his diagnosis rests on.

# Sprint Video Setup: Fix the Camera, Let the Athlete Run Through the Frame

**What it is** — Moyer's capture advice, given to participants in Live 1 after some of their clips came back blurry:

- **Fix the camera; don't pan.** Set it far enough back and have the athlete run past. For acceleration, film the first **10–20 yards**; for upright running, film **fly sprints** as they pass. A moving camera can still be used, but a fixed one is better.
- **Give yourself distance.** The good clips came from an open turf field where the filmer could back up about **30 feet**; the blurry ones came from an indoor track with a wall or railing about three feet away.
- **Film from more than one side.** Side view, plus **front and back**: stand in the lane, have the athlete run straight at the camera, and step aside at the end.
- **Listen as well as look.** In Live 2 he adds that sound tells a lot: "stompers" who drive the foot straight down sound different from athletes with a down-and-back strike.

**Why it works** — A fixed camera keeps the background stationary, so posture and limb angles are not distorted by panning, and the same setup can be repeated for a before/after comparison. Distance reduces perspective distortion and keeps the whole stride in frame. Front and back views catch frontal-plane faults (crossover, hip drop, foot placement) a side view hides. This is standard 2D video practice; Moyer gives **no frame rate, lens, height or distance specification** beyond these rules of thumb.

**When to apply** — Before any technique analysis, baseline testing or RTP comparison. Filming at a college facility where the easy spot is the sideline next to a wall: move to open space instead. Whenever you intend to compare footage across weeks.

**When NOT to apply** — A fixed camera trades field of view for accuracy; for full 40-yard or game-speed runs you will need several fixed cameras or a pan and must accept distortion. Phone video at low frame rates will not resolve ground contact reliably at top speed; the advice is about setup, not measurement. For football-specific movement (breaking on a ball, pursuit), game or practice film from multiple angles matters more than a clean track clip.

**Example** — Summer speed testing: one phone on a tripod 30 feet off the lane at the 10-yard mark, perpendicular to the run; a second at the end of the lane facing the athlete. Each player runs two starts and two 20-yard flys through the frame. The same marks are taped down for the retest six weeks later.

**Related** — [[heuristic--how-to-watch-film]] — Myszka's agreement on multiple angles and speeds for game film. [[heuristic--sprint-problem-solving-loop]] — the loop this footage feeds.

Phone video at low frame rates will not resolve ground contact reliably at top speed; the advice is about setup, not measurement. For football-specific movement (breaking on a ball, pursuit), game or practice film from multiple angles matters more than a clean track clip.

**Example** — Summer speed testing: one phone on a tripod 30 feet off the lane at the 10-yard mark, perpendicular to the run; a second at the end of the lane facing the athlete. Each player runs two starts and two 20-yard flys through the frame. The same marks are taped down for the retest six weeks later.

**Related** — [[heuristic--how-to-watch-film]] — Myszka's agreement on multiple angles and speeds for game film. [[heuristic--sprint-problem-solving-loop]] — the loop this footage feeds.

# No Full Knee Extension at Sprint Toe-Off (Contested)

**What it is** — Moyer's firm position in Live 2: **"there is no knee extension when we sprint — the knee should not extend."** At toe-off the knee stays slightly flexed and the push comes through the **hip and ankle**; the knee is roughly "frozen" from touchdown to toe-off. Details from the exchange:

- He cites a *Soviet Sports Review* article: extending the knee from **164° to 168°** "to its full capacity is a useless movement," so the knee angle at the end of takeoff at maximum speed **should not exceed 165°**. He then refuses to give ranges to coaches, so they do not chase a number.
- **Acceleration:** the first step may extend; **from step two on** it should not fully extend either.
- **Diagnosis:** visible knee extension means the athlete is not using the ankle well — "weak in the calves and feet" — and it costs energy and creates "leaping."
- He names the rival idea directly: **"delayed knee extension,"** attributed to David Grey and Joel Smith, which he says "doesn't make sense."

**Why it works** — The argument is energetic: once the leg is nearly straight, further knee extension adds little push-off length and wastes time on the ground, while hip and ankle extension do the propulsive work. That is reasonable for **upright** sprinting. The **causal diagnosis** ("extension means weak calves") is **untested** — it is Moyer's clinical inference, and other causes (posture, intent, fatigue, coaching cues) are not considered.

**Why contested** — Moyer names an opposing school. The Live 2 "pushback" was mostly participants **checking their understanding** ("even as early as step two?") and paraphrasing back in agreement, not recorded disagreement. The contest lies in the wider field: early acceleration steps commonly show near-full knee extension at toe-off in fast athletes, and "delayed knee extension" is a live coaching model. His step-two rule is stricter than much acceleration practice.

**When to apply** — Upright, flying sprints: a clearly locked knee at toe-off, with long ground contacts and a bounding look, is worth investigating, starting with calf and foot strength. Watching a player who "leaps" rather than runs at top speed.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not coach football players out of knee extension in the first steps of a start, where force needs pushing horizontally over longer contacts; the course gives no acceleration data to back the step-two rule. Do not apply the 165° figure as a threshold; it rests on one translated article no one can easily check, and Moyer himself warns against it. And do not assume the calf is the cause without testing it.

**Example** — A linebacker's 20-yard fly shows a straight knee at toe-off and a floaty stride. Before cueing, the staff tests single-leg calf strength and finds a large deficit on one side from an old ankle sprain; that becomes the first target. His 10-yard start, which also shows extension on steps one to three, is left alone.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-joint-actions-by-phase]] — the toe-off cell this disputes. [[claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]] — the ankle claim his diagnosis rests on.

=== principle--watch-them-run-in-sprint-return-to-play
**What it is** — Moyer's complaint from years in an orthopaedic practice: rehab clinics treat a running injury (patellar pain, a hamstring strain) with generic exercises — TKEs, knee extensions, Nordics, bridges, isometrics, then a short-to-long running programme — **without ever watching the athlete run**. The pain goes, the athlete "goes back to running like crap", and the injury returns. His process instead: (1) gather **injury history, training background and current goals**; (2) know the **sport's demands**; (3) **watch and film them run** before choosing interventions; (4) **re-film after** the rehab block to see whether mechanics or left-right differences actually changed. He states that "gym strength is less important than how they apply force to the ground during running", so a running-specific test is essential for judging progress.
**When NOT to apply** — Film shows *how* they run, not tissue readiness; it does not replace strength, range, imaging or clinical criteria, and "runs well" is not a clearance test. Changing mechanics during late rehab also adds a new stressor at a vulnerable time — record mechanics, but be careful about making big technique changes in the final days before clearance. His injury statistics (25–35% of team-sport injuries are hamstrings, "some show 50%") were quoted loosely.
=== heuristic--film-several-sprints-before-judging-mechanics
**What it is** — Moyer's filming habits, stated in passing rather than as a protocol. He never judges an athlete on **one sprint from one view**; he wants a set of sprints from different angles (side-on for the stride, front and rear for foot, ankle and pelvis). He **records the conditions** that could distort the picture — his first film of a pro football player was on a **wet track in flat basketball shoes**, so he told himself to "take it with a grain of salt". He notes the **intent** of the run: timed sprints, where the athlete is chasing a number, can look different from drill work. He watches live first for the global picture, then breaks the film down (Dartfish or a phone) for the key actions. In the live session he adds that from the front or back he always reads **from the ground up**.
**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: it is sensible practice, but the course gives no protocol — no frame rate, camera height, distance, or number of reps. Build those yourself and keep them fixed, or before/after comparisons are not comparable. Watching live for "global" impressions is quick but unreliable at full speed; do not act on live impressions alone.

# Return to Play Should Examine the Movement Pattern Present at Injury

**What it is** — Moyer's claim: **the mechanism of injury is often the way the athlete moves**, yet return-to-play processes usually isolate the injured joint, restore tissue capacity, and progress a short-to-long running program without ever filming how the athlete runs, throws or cuts. His Live 1 line: *"you can have a great 10-by-10 running program, but if they run like shit you're just going to have another chance of getting hurt again."* He goes further: he suspects the reason **previous injury is the strongest predictor of future injury** is that the faulty movement is never addressed.

**Why it works** — The logic: if a movement fault loaded the tissue to failure once, a stronger tissue running the same pattern is still exposed. That is plausible, but **every causal link here is asserted, not shown**. The "previous injury predicts injury *because* we ignore movement" step is Moyer's inference; previous injury predicts re-injury through many routes (incomplete healing, scar tissue, deconditioning, early return, structural change). His evidence is clinical experience as an orthopaedic-practice RTP specialist and one case — a 16-year-old quarterback's elbow fracture on a throw, followed by surgery, rehab and eight months of mechanics work with Yessis — where all three changed at once.

**When to apply** — Late-stage RTP for a hamstring strain in a skill player: film the athlete sprinting before clearance and compare with pre-injury footage if it exists. A second soft-tissue injury in the same region. A throwing-arm injury with no contact mechanism. Add a filmed movement check to the RTP criteria, alongside, not instead of, tissue and capacity criteria.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a reason to delay tissue-based progression or to override the medical team. Many good RTP frameworks already include movement-quality checks, so the specific add here is **filming the movement that injured the athlete**, not "look at movement" in general. Contact injuries (a tackle to the knee) have no running-mechanics cause to correct. And changing mechanics late in rehab adds a new motor-learning load at the moment the athlete is least robust; timing matters.

**Example** — A corner strains his hamstring at top speed. Tissue criteria are met at week four. Before clearance, the staff films a 30-yard fly from the side and sees him landing well in front of the hips with a long swing-leg lever. They keep the RTP running progression but add targeted technical work and refilm before full practice.

**Related** — [[heuristic--sprint-problem-solving-loop]] — the general loop this applies to rehab. [[heuristic--sprint-video-setup-stationary-camera]] — how to capture comparable footage.

# Sprint Video Setup: Fix the Camera, Let the Athlete Run Through the Frame

**What it is** — Moyer's capture advice, given to participants in Live 1 after some of their clips came back blurry:

- **Fix the camera; don't pan.** Set it far enough back and have the athlete run past. For acceleration, film the first **10–20 yards**; for upright running, film **fly sprints** as they pass. A moving camera can still be used, but a fixed one is better.
- **Give yourself distance.** The good clips came from an open turf field where the filmer could back up about **30 feet**; the blurry ones came from an indoor track with a wall or railing about three feet away.
- **Film from more than one side.** Side view, plus **front and back**: stand in the lane, have the athlete run straight at the camera, and step aside at the end.
- **Listen as well as look.** In Live 2 he adds that sound tells a lot: "stompers" who drive the foot straight down sound different from athletes with a down-and-back strike.

**Why it works** — A fixed camera keeps the background stationary, so posture and limb angles are not distorted by panning, and the same setup can be repeated for a before/after comparison. Distance reduces perspective distortion and keeps the whole stride in frame. Front and back views catch frontal-plane faults (crossover, hip drop, foot placement) a side view hides. This is standard 2D video practice; Moyer gives **no frame rate, lens, height or distance specification** beyond these rules of thumb.

**When to apply** — Before any technique analysis, baseline testing or RTP comparison. Filming at a college facility where the easy spot is the sideline next to a wall: move to open space instead. Whenever you intend to compare footage across weeks.

**When NOT to apply** — A fixed camera trades field of view for accuracy; for full 40-yard or game-speed runs you will need several fixed cameras or a pan and must accept distortion. Phone video at low frame rates will not resolve ground contact reliably at top speed; the advice is about setup, not measurement. For football-specific movement (breaking on a ball, pursuit), game or practice film from multiple angles matters more than a clean track clip.

**Example** — Summer speed testing: one phone on a tripod 30 feet off the lane at the 10-yard mark, perpendicular to the run; a second at the end of the lane facing the athlete. Each player runs two starts and two 20-yard flys through the frame. The same marks are taped down for the retest six weeks later.

**Related** — [[heuristic--how-to-watch-film]] — Myszka's agreement on multiple angles and speeds for game film. [[heuristic--sprint-problem-solving-loop]] — the loop this footage feeds.

# Sprint Problem-Solving Loop: Watch the Movement, Then Work Backwards

**What it is** — Moyer's organising idea for the whole course. Start with **how the athlete actually moves on the field**, not with the weight room or a drill menu, and work backwards: **observe the sport movement → name the constraint → intervene → look again**. The constraint can be **technical** (a sequencing error) or **physical** — his Live 2 example is a poor frontside/knee-drive action that may be a weak hip-flexor/lower-abdominal contribution rather than a coaching problem, so the fix is strength work for that joint action, not another cue. His one-line version from Live 1: *"drills are meant for solving problems — if you don't do an assessment, what problem are you trying to solve?"* Technology (video software, force plates) is there to **quantify what the eye already saw** and to sell the plan to coaches and parents; it does not "drive the bus."

**Why it works** — It forces the intervention to answer a named fault, so every drill has a reason and a test. The mechanism is ordinary diagnostic logic, not a sprint-specific finding. Moyer's own framing — that the weight room is where staffs hold a "PhD" and on-field movement is where they hold a "GED" — is a provocation, not a measured claim. Note the **recheck step is thin in the transcript**: it appears mainly as his demand, in Live 2, to "show me the before, tell me the intervention, show me the after," rather than as a defined retest protocol.

**When to apply** — Any speed block where drills were chosen before anyone filmed the athletes. A skill player whose 10-yard time stalls while his lifts climb. An RTP athlete cleared on tissue criteria who has not been filmed sprinting. Deciding whether a mechanics fault gets a cue or a strength exercise.

**When NOT to apply** — The loop presumes the observer can reliably see the constraint; Moyer's eye rests on 20 years and a mentorship with Michael Yessis, and he offers no reliability data for it. For a new staff member, "trust your eye over the software" is the wrong starting rule — use the video to *train* the eye. And for a large team with limited coaching time, a sound general speed program run for everyone may beat individual diagnosis for most athletes; the loop earns its cost on the athletes whose times or injury history say something is wrong.

**Example** — A slot receiver with a slow first 10 yards. Filming shows a low, short knee drive. Rather than adding A-skips, the staff checks whether hip-flexor strength and endurance at the relevant range are the limit, adds that work for four weeks, and refilms the same start from the same camera spot.

**Related** — [[heuristic--sprint-video-setup-stationary-camera]] — how to shoot the "observe" and "recheck" footage so they are comparable. [[claim--hip-flexor-fatigue-degrades-sprint-mechanics]] — the physical-limit example he leans on.

# Essential vs. Non-Essential Variables in Sprint Observation

**What it is** — Moyer's bridge from Bernstein to what a coach should watch and coach in a sprint. Bernstein: to solve a motor problem the organism separates **essential variables** (actively controlled, protected against environmental disturbance) from **non-essential variables** (allowed to yield and adapt) — "active toward the former, reactive toward the latter." Verkhoshansky, Bernstein's student, renamed these **key movements** (which produce the power output of the skill) and **secondary movements** (which assist them). Moyer's application:

- **Coach the key movements; let the secondary ones vary.** In sprinting he names three key movements (knee drive, pawback, ankle extension) and treats the arms as secondary.
- **"We have to coach to something."** Against a purely self-organising, constraints-only approach, he argues there is no ideal model but there *are* key actions every good sprinter shares.
- **His reading of Bernstein's blacksmith:** the hammer took 100 different paths, but the **same joint actions** (shoulder, elbow, wrist) occurred each time. Trajectory varies; joint actions do not.

**Why it works** — It gives the observer a filter: variation in a secondary movement is noise to be tolerated, variation in a key movement is a fault to address. That matches Bernstein's idea and is consistent with the variability literature. **The list of what counts as "key" in sprinting is Moyer's judgement**, inherited from Verkhoshansky and Yessis, not an empirically derived set. His blacksmith reading is an interpretation; the ecological camp would say joint-action invariance at that coarse level is compatible with their view, so the disagreement is narrower than he presents.

**When to apply** — Deciding what to cue after watching a player sprint. Settling staff arguments about "ugly" sprinters: if the key actions are sound, leave the style alone. Explaining to a skill coach why a player's odd arm carriage is not the priority.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a licence to groove one technique: he concedes there is no ideal model and everyone runs differently. It is sprint-specific; in football, reactive tasks (pursuit angles, cuts) have different essentials, often perceptual, that this framework does not cover. And he cites Rob Gray as "late to the game" on coaching to something; that is his characterisation of a debate, not a settled result.

**Example** — Two receivers both have wild arm action. One also lands with a straight, stiff-kneed reach and slow ground contacts; the other has a fast, high knee drive and a quick down-and-back strike. The framework says fix the first receiver's leg action and leave the second one's arms alone.
